title: Generosity
hookLine: give more than you need to
tomorrow: why would a Bible law care what's in a merchant's bag?

cards: A man outside the grocery store asks for a couple of dollars. A fundraiser link lands in the family group chat. Two instincts show up at once: just give, or find out more first.
Give to everyone who asks, or know who you're giving to? Both instincts have roots in the Church, and both can point to old words. One side says a gift should be quick.
The other says it should be careful. So let each side make its case.

teach.b: The first side opens with Jesus himself, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Give to him that asketh of thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not away." No background check.
And when he describes how God gives back, the measure spills: "good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over." That's generosity as more than needed, past the edge of the cup.
The second side opens with the Didache, an early Christian teaching manual.

teach.h: LET IT SWEAT IN YOUR HANDS.
teach.b: It quotes that same command to give to everyone who asks, and then sets a saying beside it: let your gift sweat in your hands until you know who you're giving to.
The saying doesn't cancel the command; it sits right beside it. The book of Ecclesiasticus says something close: if you do good, know to whom you do it. Giving as care, not as a reflex.
The Church keeps both sides in the room. Wide giving guards against a heart that's always looking for a reason not to. Careful giving guards against help that doesn't help.
And on one thing both sides agree, with Paul: give "not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The argument is about how. Neither side argues for giving less.

how: Catholics give alms both directly, to people who ask, and through parishes and charities such as the Society of St. Vincent de Paul, and Lent sets almsgiving beside prayer and fasting.

o: paying back exactly what you owe
giving only to people who earn it

s: Jesus says to check that someone deserves it before you give
Matthew 5: give to him that asketh of thee. the caution comes from other early sources.
an early Christian manual says to let your gift sweat in your hands
the Didache, right after it quotes the command to give to everyone who asks.
Paul says giving only counts if it hurts
not with sadness, or of necessity: God loveth a cheerful giver.

games.q: Mia says give to anyone who asks, no questions. your dad says give through the shelter so it's used well. what's the strongest case for your dad's side?
o: an early Christian manual: let the gift sweat in your hands until you know who it's for.
people who ask on the street mostly don't need it; the shelter knows who does.
Jesus told his followers to give only to people who deserve it.
games.why: Dad's side has the Didache and Ecclesiasticus: give with care. Mia's side has Jesus's own words: give to him that asketh. the Church keeps both, and neither side argues for giving less.

practice: Sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up, the way you'd hold out a gift. Bring to mind one place where you could give a little past what's expected: a tip, a donation, an hour of your time.
Stay with that open posture until the giving feels glad rather than owed. If you pray, you can ask for a glad heart in the giving.

wordCard.voice: Generosity. Giving past what's required, wide and wise, with a glad heart, the measure pressed down, shaken together and running over.

orig.note: Greek: cheerful, glad. Paul's word for the giver God loves.

carryVoice: Your line: more than needed. In Luke the measure is pressed down, shaken, and still spills over the edge. Back tomorrow.
